cards.explanation: The answer is that Agrippa gives Paul permission to speak for himself. King Agrippa tells him, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” That's the green light. Paul is the one who gets to speak, friends.
The answer is True. Agrippa gives permission, then Paul stretches out his hand and begins his defense. He's about to speak for himself, and he starts with his hand stretched out.

The answer is that the king knows Jewish customs well. Paul says it plainly: “…you are acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies.” The charges come from the Jews, so a king who knows those customs can follow what Paul is talking about. It's like explaining a work mix-up to a coworker who already knows how your office runs.

The answer is Pharisee. Paul says he “…lived as a Pharisee, adhering to the strictest sect of our religion.” He says the same thing about himself in Philippians 3:5. If anyone knew the rulebook, friends, it was him.

The answer is his hope in God's promise to their fathers. Paul says, “…I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers…” He adds that the twelve tribes are hoping to see that promise fulfilled as they serve God day and night. So the charge, in Paul's telling, comes down to hope.
The word is raises. Paul asks, “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” Notice the words “…any of you…” That's a bold way to put a question, friends.

The answer is True. Paul says it himself: “…I put many of the saints in prison, and when they were condemned to death, I cast my vote against them.” That was with authority from the chief priests. Paul isn't hiding any of it, and I respect that.

The answer is “Why do you persecute Me?” The voice says, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” Saul was going after the saints, and the voice says it's Him he's persecuting. I think hearing my own name called twice from heaven would stop me in my tracks.

The answer is Jesus. Paul asks, “Who are You, Lord?” and the answer comes: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…” Paul had been working against the name of Jesus of Nazareth, and now he hears that name from the Lord Himself. That's a real turning point for him.

The word is witness. Jesus says, “…I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a witness of what you have seen from Me and what I will show you.” A witness tells what he has seen. So Saul gets sent out with something real to report.

The answer is an inheritance. Jesus says they may receive “…forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.” So forgiveness and an inheritance sit together in one sentence. That's two gifts, friends.
The answer is False. Paul says he declared that they should “…repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance.” So repentance was meant to show up in what people do.

The answer is that the Christ would suffer and rise first from the dead. Paul says the prophets and Moses said “…that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.” So suffering and rising are both in the plan. Paul says he's adding nothing beyond what they said.

The answer is False. Paul says the Christ would “…proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.” The Gentiles, the non-Jewish nations, are named right there. Israel gets the light, and so do they.

The answer is his great learning. Festus, the governor, shouts, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” He blames the learning, not the chains or the road. That's a strange compliment dressed up as an insult.

The answer is False. Paul says, “I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.” So he says the very opposite of a hidden corner. In his words, these events were not done in a corner.

The answer is that Agrippa asks if Paul can persuade him to become a Christian that fast. Agrippa asks, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” Paul had just said, “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.” I think that question hit close, but the text doesn't tell us what was in Agrippa's heart.

The answer is that they would all become what he is. Paul says, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.” He's wishing for the king AND everyone listening. He doesn't wish for the chains, friends, and who could blame him?

The answer is False. On their way out, the king and the others say to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” So the statement is false, because they say the opposite. Imprisonment is right there in what they say he has not done anything worthy of.

The answer is Caesar. Agrippa tells Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.” Paul had made that appeal himself earlier (Acts 25:11). So the appeal to Caesar is the very thing Agrippa names.
